list_one.title: A 32-bit length taken from the wire sizes a byte array before any payload arrives (ValueReader.readBytes)
list_one.impact: A peer that speaks to this decoder can make the client JVM commit up to ~2 GiB of heap per value, at a cost of five bytes per attempt and with no payload to send. The result is OutOfMemoryError in the process hosting the client library, which is the consuming application, not merely the broker connection — a Java OOM is not contained to the thread that triggered it, and repeated attempts hold the allocation attempt for as long as the collector fights for the space. Availability of the whole client application is the asset at risk. The same shape appears inside a field table, where the enclosing TruncatedInputStream cannot help: a table whose declared length is six bytes can still carry `x` plus a declared length of 2147483646, and the array is allocated before the truncated stream refuses the read.

list_one.title: An untrusted 64-bit timestamp is multiplied by 1000 with no overflow check
list_one.impact: The peer obtains Date values outside the range the seconds encoding is supposed to be able to express, including a far-past date from a far-future input. Consuming code that treats a message timestamp as age, freshness or expiry receives a value that does not round-trip. The attacker gains almost nothing they did not already have — an AMQP timestamp is peer-supplied by design, so any in-range value was already theirs to choose — which is why this is recorded as informational rather than as a risk.
list_one.evidence: Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. The eight bytes come from the stream and the product is computed in `long` arithmetic, which wraps silently in Java. Any seconds value above 9223372036854775 (or below its negative) produces a millisecond value with the opposite sign or an unrelated magnitude. Reached from the public readTimestamp() at lines 274-278 and from readFieldValue case 'T' at line 178. This is the third neighbour WEB-26 names in the same family — a value multiplied without an overflow check — and it sits in the same file as F-001 and F-002.

list_one.title: Mutual recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray carries no depth counter
list_one.impact: A few tens of kilobytes of nested field arrays exhausts the JVM stack and raises StackOverflowError. That is an Error, not the IOException the surrounding code is written to handle: nothing in this class catches it, so it unwinds past the decode loop and kills the thread that reads the connection rather than closing the connection cleanly. The consuming application is left with a dead reader thread, which is a harder failure to detect and recover from than a protocol error. Depth also multiplies the memory cost of F-001, since each level can declare its own oversized value.
list_one.evidence:
The cycle closes twice, both times on data the peer chooses:

  readFieldValue (line 158) -- case 'F' (line 180) --> readTable (line 139) --> readFieldValue (line 150)
  readFieldValue (line 158) -- case 'A' (line 183) --> readArray (line 237) --> readFieldValue (line 245)

The three signatures are `static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)` (158), `private static Map<String, Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)` (139) and `private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)` (237). None carries a depth parameter, and no counter is kept anywhere in the class — WEB-26's test is exactly this: walk the recursive entry points and look for a depth argument in the signature. Each additional level of nesting costs the peer five bytes inside a field array (the type octet 'A' plus a four-byte length) or six inside a table (a zero-length short string name, the octet 'F', a four-byte length). The recursion is driven by `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)` (line 244) and `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` (line 148), neither of which bounds nesting.

list_one.title: The build generates and ships protocol classes from a working copy the manifest neither pins nor verifies
list_one.impact: The generated AMQP protocol classes are compiled into the published jar, so whoever controls the contents of the codegen working copy on the build machine chooses source code that ships to every consumer, without that change appearing in this repository's diff. This is the shape of a build-path compromise rather than a demonstrated one: reaching it requires write access to the build host or to whatever clones that directory, so no attacker outside the build environment is claimed here.
list_one.evidence: pom.xml:102-112 declares `deps.dir` = `${basedir}/deps` and `codegen.dir` = `${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen`, documented in the same comment as "a directory containing a working copy of rabbitmq-codegen and rabbitmq-server". pom.xml:597-637 binds groovy-maven-plugin to `generate-sources` to run `generate_amqp_sources.groovy`, described in its own comment as "a proxy to execute a Python script" — `${basedir}/codegen.py` — against `${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json`, writing AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java into `${project.build.directory}/generated-sources`. pom.xml:640-658 then adds that directory to the main compile through build-helper-maven-plugin `add-source`. The plugin runs Groovy 2.4.21, injected as a plugin dependency at pom.xml:81 and 665-668. What the manifest pins is `codegen.spec_version` 0.9.1, which selects a file name; it declares no revision, checksum or signature for the working copy that file comes from, and the step that obtains that working copy is not in the manifest at all.

list_two.title: A repeated field name in a table is dropped silently, first occurrence wins
list_two.impact: Nothing on its own, and no exploit path is claimed here. It is recorded because duplicate-key handling is where header smuggling lives when two implementations disagree: a decoder that took the last occurrence would build a different map from the same bytes, and only one of the two would match what a signature, a broker-side filter or a second consumer saw.

list_two.title: A declared table or array length is never compared with the bytes that remain
list_two.impact: An over-declared length is not an error here, it is a licence to read further. A nested table or array that declares more bytes than its parent holds keeps consuming until the underlying stream ends, so it absorbs the sibling fields that followed it; the parent loop at line 148 then sees `available() == 0` and returns a map that silently lost them, with no MalformedFrameException raised. A decoder that validated the declared length against the enclosing region would reject the same frame. The result is a parser differential: this client and any stricter peer disagree about which headers a message carries, which matters wherever an application routes, filters, audits or authorizes on a header value.

list_two.title: The timestamp field multiplies a wire-chosen 64-bit value by 1000 unchecked
list_two.impact: The peer chooses which side of the epoch the decoded Date lands on, independently of the value it declared. Where a consumer compares that Date against now — message expiry, a deduplication or replay window, retention, ordering, an audit record — a wrapped value inverts the comparison, and the audit trail records a time the sender never sent.

list_two.title: Field tables and field arrays recurse with no depth counter anywhere in the chain
list_two.impact: A single frame of a few tens of kilobytes buys thousands of nesting levels, which is StackOverflowError in the thread decoding the frame. That is an Error, not an IOException: the `catch (IOException)` and MalformedFrameException handling the protocol layer is written around does not catch it, so the failure surfaces as a dead connection-reading thread rather than as a rejected frame. Each level also allocates a HashMap or ArrayList and two stream wrappers, so the same bytes buy a heap multiple on the way down.
list_two.evidence:
The cycle is closed and carries no depth argument in any of the three signatures:
  static Object readFieldValue(DataInputStream in)            // line 158
      case 'F': value = readTable(in);                        // line 181
      case 'A': value = readArray(in);                        // line 184
  private static Map<String,Object> readTable(DataInputStream in)   // line 139
      while(tableIn.available() > 0) { readShortstr(tableIn); readFieldValue(tableIn); }   // lines 148-152
  private static List<Object> readArray(DataInputStream in)   // line 237
      while(arrayIn.available() > 0) { array.add(readFieldValue(arrayIn)); }               // lines 244-247
One nesting level costs the sender five bytes: the type tag 'F' or 'A' plus a four-byte length. Nothing in the file counts levels, and no cap is passed in from the public entry point readTable() at line 252.

list_two.title: A four-byte length off the wire sizes the byte array before any content is read
list_two.impact: A peer that spends four bytes makes the decoding process commit up to ~2 GiB of heap before it can fail. readFully() then throws EOFException, but the array already exists; repeated across frames or connections this is OutOfMemoryError or sustained GC pressure in the application embedding the library, with no data or credential needed by the sender. The same line also converts an over-large length into UnsupportedOperationException — an unchecked exception on a decode path whose callers are declared to throw IOException, so it escapes protocol error handling instead of being reported as a malformed frame.

list_two.title: Shipped API source is generated from a build input the manifest never verifies
list_two.impact: Part of the published artifact's source is decided by a directory that is not in this repository and is not checked against anything — the spec is selected by file name and a version string, not by content. Whoever populates `deps/rabbitmq_codegen` in a build environment influences generated public API code without a reviewable change in this tree. No attacker path is claimed: this is the integrity of a build input, and it is recorded as one.
list_two.evidence:
pom.xml lines 110-112 declare the input outside the module:
    <deps.dir>${basedir}/deps</deps.dir>
    <codegen.dir>${deps.dir}/rabbitmq_codegen</codegen.dir>
    <codegen.spec_version>0.9.1</codegen.spec_version>
Lines 613-636 run it at generate-sources through groovy-maven-plugin, goal `execute`, with `<script>${basedir}/codegen.py</script>` and `<spec>${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json</spec>`, writing com/rabbitmq/client/AMQP.java and com/rabbitmq/client/impl/AMQImpl.java; lines 644-656 add that directory to the main source root with build-helper `add-source`. The comment at lines 102-108 says the directory should hold a working copy of another repository. Nothing in the manifest pins a commit or a digest, and no verification step precedes the execution.
